cards.front: What is USUCAPIO (usucaption) and what does it achieve?
cards.back:
Acquisition of civil-law ownership through uninterrupted qualified possession over a statutory period.
• Original acquisition: the former owner loses his right
• Prevents a permanent separation of possession and ownership
• Rewards the good-faith possessor once the time has elapsed

cards.front: Which three forms of USUCAPIO does the textbook distinguish by function?
cards.back:
Usucaption curing (1) a form defect, (2) a legal deficiency of the transferor, (3) a dormant inheritance.
• (1) RES MANCIPI conveyed without MANCIPATIO or IN IURE CESSIO
• (2) e.g. transferor not owner, or lacking capacity
• (3) USUCAPIO PRO HEREDE: overt taking, then one year's possession

cards.front: In which two typical situations does a form defect lead to usucaption?
cards.back:
Occupation of an ownerless RES MANCIPI, and simple TRADITIO (delivery) of a RES MANCIPI by the owner with IUSTA CAUSA.
• Acquirer first becomes only bonitarian owner
• Civil-law ownership after one year (movables) or two years (land)
• Meanwhile transferor keeps the bare NUDUM IUS QUIRITIUM

cards.front: Bonitarian owner vs. mere usucapient — why is not every usucapient a bonitarian owner?
cards.back:
Only someone who received a RES MANCIPI from an authorised person (mere form defect) becomes bonitarian owner.
• Acquirer from an unauthorised vendor is merely a usucapient
• Bonitarian owner has in substance the strongest right
• His action: ACTIO PUBLICIANA (civil owner: REI VINDICATIO)

cards.topic: 28.10. USUCAPIO — RES HABILIS, TITULUS, BONA FIDES, POSSESSIO, TEMPUS
cards.front: Which three categories of legal deficiency relating to the transferor can USUCAPIO cure?
cards.back:
Lack of ownership or authority, lack of transactional capacity, and lack of a valid CAUSA (legal ground).
• (a) transferor neither owner nor authorised to dispose
• (b) PUPILLUS, FURIOSUS, PRODIGUS acting without guardian
• (c) capable parties but no valid causal agreement

cards.topic: 28.10. USUCAPIO — RES HABILIS, TITULUS, BONA FIDES, POSSESSIO, TEMPUS
cards.front: What does NEMO PLUS IURIS TRANSFERRE POTEST QUAM IPSE HABET mean for a TRADITIO by a non-owner?
cards.back:
Nobody can transfer more rights than he has: the transferee gets possession, not ownership.
• Applies where the transferor lacked ownership or authority of disposal
• USUCAPIO can cure this defect over time

cards.topic: 28.10. USUCAPIO — RES HABILIS, TITULUS, BONA FIDES, POSSESSIO, TEMPUS
cards.front: Why does acquisition from a PUPILLUS, FURIOSUS or PRODIGUS without the guardian's consent fail?
cards.back:
They own the thing but lack transactional capacity, so there is no IUSTA CAUSA TRADITIONIS.
• PRODIGUS: spendthrift barred by the praetor from alienating
• NEGOTIUM CLAUDICANS: the part conferring rights on them stays valid
• A buyer unaware of the incapacity may usucapt

cards.topic: 28.10. USUCAPIO — RES HABILIS, TITULUS, BONA FIDES, POSSESSIO, TEMPUS
cards.front: Which five requirements must USUCAPIO for a legal deficiency meet, as the textbook names them?
cards.back:
RES HABILIS, TITULUS, BONA FIDES, POSSESSIO, TEMPUS.
• RES HABILIS = thing capable of usucaption; TITULUS = legal title
• BONA FIDES = good faith; POSSESSIO = possession
• TEMPUS = period of time prescribed by law

cards.topic: 28.10. USUCAPIO — RES HABILIS, TITULUS, BONA FIDES, POSSESSIO, TEMPUS
cards.front: Which things are not RES HABILIS, i.e. cannot be usucapted?
cards.back:
Things outside private commerce and stolen goods; later also things obtained by force.
• RES EXTRA COMMERCIUM: RES PUBLICAE (market square), RES DIVINI IURIS (temple)
• RES FURTIVAE (stolen goods): barred by the LEX ATINIA
• LEGES IULIAE ET PLAUTIAE: things taken by force, including land

cards.topic: 28.10. USUCAPIO — RES HABILIS, TITULUS, BONA FIDES, POSSESSIO, TEMPUS
cards.front: What is the IUSTA CAUSA USUCAPIONIS?
cards.back:
A title that would have conferred ownership had the thing come from an authorised transferor.
• Equivalent to the IUSTA CAUSA TRADITIONIS of derivative acquisition
• Largely dispensed with: acquisition from incapable persons, putative titles

cards.topic: 28.10. USUCAPIO — RES HABILIS, TITULUS, BONA FIDES, POSSESSIO, TEMPUS
cards.front: What is a putative title, and how do Roman jurists view it?
cards.back:
An apparent CAUSA the acquirer wrongly believes valid; jurists disagree whether it suffices.
• Strict: valid IUSTA CAUSA required (Ulpian D 41.3.27)
• Middle: rejected for sale, accepted otherwise (PRO DOTE, PRO SUO)
• Liberal: excusable error (TOLERABILIS ERROR) suffices even for sale

cards.topic: 28.10. USUCAPIO — RES HABILIS, TITULUS, BONA FIDES, POSSESSIO, TEMPUS
cards.front: What is the content of the usucapient's BONA FIDES (good faith)?
cards.back:
A mistake about facts at acquisition, e.g. not knowing the transferor lacks ownership, authority or capacity.
• A legal error (error of law) excludes BONA FIDES
• Only concrete knowledge is MALA FIDES; mere doubts do not harm
• No duty to investigate (modern law: no negligence)

cards.topic: 28.10. USUCAPIO — RES HABILIS, TITULUS, BONA FIDES, POSSESSIO, TEMPUS
cards.front: What does MALA FIDES SUPERVENIENS NON NOCET mean for USUCAPIO?
cards.back:
Bad faith arising later does no harm: BONA FIDES is needed only at the moment of acquisition.
• Re-acquired possession requires fresh BONA FIDES
• Disputed for fruits: Pomponius/Paulus vs Julian

cards.topic: 28.10. USUCAPIO — RES HABILIS, TITULUS, BONA FIDES, POSSESSIO, TEMPUS
cards.front: Paulus D 41.4.2.15 (Case 86): two buyers from a minor without his tutor — one thinks him of age, one thinks minors may alienate. Who can usucapt?
cards.back:
Only the first buyer: he errs about facts, the second errs about law.
• Factual error (age) → BONA FIDES, usucaption possible
• Legal error (minors' capacity) → no usucaption

cards.topic: 28.10. USUCAPIO — RES HABILIS, TITULUS, BONA FIDES, POSSESSIO, TEMPUS
cards.front: Which requirements does USUCAPIO place on POSSESSIO?
cards.back:
Possession must be unflawed (IUSTA POSSESSIO: not VI, CLAM, PRECARIO) and uninterrupted for the whole period.
• Mediate possession through a detentor suffices
• Loss ends usucaption; regained possession restarts it
• Meanwhile: ACTIO PUBLICIANA to recover possession

cards.topic: 28.10. USUCAPIO — RES HABILIS, TITULUS, BONA FIDES, POSSESSIO, TEMPUS
cards.front: How long is the TEMPUS, and does a predecessor's possession count?
cards.back:
One year for movables, two years for immovables, counted from acquiring possession.
• A buyer must start anew (ACCESSIO TEMPORIS only post-classical)
• Heirs continue the deceased's usucaption (SUCCESSIO IN POSSESSIONEM)
• Heirs need not be BONA FIDE

cards.topic: 28.10. USUCAPIO — RES HABILIS, TITULUS, BONA FIDES, POSSESSIO, TEMPUS
cards.front: Exegesis: a Digest fragment is about USUCAPIO — which questions should your interpretation address?
cards.back:
First ask why derivative acquisition failed, then test the five requirements.
• Form defect or legal deficiency (ownership, capacity, CAUSA)?
• RES HABILIS (LEX ATINIA, REVERSIO)? Valid TITULUS or putative title?
• BONA FIDES at acquisition (fact vs law)? Unflawed POSSESSIO, TEMPUS complete?

cards.topic: 28.10. USUCAPIO — LEX ATINIA and modern bona fide acquisition
cards.front: What does the LEX ATINIA provide?
cards.back:
Stolen goods (RES FURTIVAE) cannot be usucapted until they return into the owner's POTESTAS (power).
• Binds the thief and all later acquirers, even in good faith
• Not for land, which cannot be stolen
• Blemish removed by REVERSIO IN POTESTATEM

cards.topic: 28.10. USUCAPIO — LEX ATINIA and modern bona fide acquisition
cards.front: When has a REVERSIO IN POTESTATEM occurred?
cards.back:
When the owner regains immediate custody of the stolen thing and recognises it as his own.
• Not enough: recovery via a steward, or return to the detentor
• Furtivity also ends if owner receives its value (Case 79)
• Afterwards a BONA FIDE acquirer may usucapt

cards.topic: 28.10. USUCAPIO — LEX ATINIA and modern bona fide acquisition
cards.front: Pledgor A steals his pledged thing back from creditor B — can it now be usucapted (Cases 74, 75)?
cards.back:
Disputed: Cassius/Paulus say yes, Labeo only after its return to the pledgee.
• Case 74: thing is back in the owner's POTESTAS, though A is FUR
• Case 75: pledgee's right weighs more; owner's theft blocks usucaption

cards.topic: 28.10. USUCAPIO — LEX ATINIA and modern bona fide acquisition
cards.front: Roman USUCAPIO vs. modern bona fide acquisition — what is the difference?
cards.back:
Both protect trust in honest dealings, but bona fide acquisition gives ownership immediately, without TEMPUS.
• Acquirer from an unauthorised vendor gets original ownership
• Mainly movables (Austria: land only via register or usucaption)

cards.topic: 28.10. USUCAPIO — LEX ATINIA and modern bona fide acquisition
cards.front: What are the typical requirements of modern bona fide acquisition?
cards.back:
Good faith without negligence, unflawed possession and usually a valid title, mainly for movables.
• Often consideration required (§ 367 ABGB)
• Privileged: public auction, businessman's ordinary course, entrusted goods
• Registered movables (ships, cars) may be excluded (Art 1156 Codice civile)

cards.topic: 28.10. USUCAPIO — LEX ATINIA and modern bona fide acquisition
cards.front: Stolen goods: how does modern law differ from Roman law and the LEX ATINIA?
cards.back:
Rome treats stolen goods as RES INHABILES; modern systems sometimes allow their bona fide acquisition.
• ABGB: first two cases of § 367 (auction, businessman)
• BGB § 935(2): only auction, money, bearer bonds
• Owner may reclaim: ZGB five years, Code civil three years

cards.front: What is OCCUPATIO, and which things can be acquired by it?
cards.back:
Taking possession of a RES NULLIUS (ownerless thing); an original mode of acquisition.
• Originally ownerless things: wild animals, pearls from the seabed
• RES DERELICTAE (intentionally abandoned things)
• Treasure-trove (THESAURUS), according to the prevailing opinion

cards.front: What does OCCUPATIO of wild animals require, and when is ownership lost?
cards.back:
Open and secure possession, certainly given when the captor has direct physical control.
• Animal regains natural freedom → possession and ownership lost
• Enclosure or fish basin: owned; fenced forest or pond: not (Case 95)

cards.front: What is the CONSUETUDO REVERTENDI?
cards.back:
The habit of returning: a tamed wild animal stays owned while it habitually returns.
• Habit lost → animal wild and ownerless again
• Swarming bees are wild; a returning bee or pigeon is owned
• Irrelevant for pets: runaway pets are not ownerless

cards.front: When is a thing derelinquished (RES DERELICTA), and what about goods jettisoned at sea?
cards.back:
When the owner abandons it intending to give up possession and ownership; anyone may then occupy it.
• Jettison in an emergency: at first only possession is lost
• In doubt, no dereliction
• Classical: occupied RES MANCIPI yields only bonitarian ownership

cards.front: Can the finder of lost property acquire ownership by OCCUPATIO or USUCAPIO?
cards.back:
No: lost but not abandoned property is not ownerless.
• Finder must give public notice to escape suspicion of FURTUM (theft)
• No usucaption: no IUSTA CAUSA, usually no BONA FIDES

cards.front: What is a THESAURUS (treasure-trove), and who owns it according to the different opinions?
cards.back:
A valuable object hidden so long that its owner can no longer be traced.
• Sabinians (prevailing): RES NULLIUS, acquired by OCCUPATIO
• Proculians: aware landowner acquires by possessory intent; older view: ACCESSIO
• Hadrian: half to the finder, half to the landowner

cards.front: What are fruits (FRUCTUS), and which kinds exist?
cards.back:
Recurring goods or income derived from a thing without diminishing its substance.
• FRUCTUS NATURALES (milk, wool, eggs) and FRUCTUS CIVILES (rent)
• Animal offspring is a fruit; PARTUS ANCILLAE (slave's child) is not
• Before separation: dependent part of the fruit-bearing thing

cards.front: Who acquires fruits, and at which moment?
cards.back:
Owner, bona fide possessor and EMPHYTEUTA (hereditary lessee) acquire at SEPARATIO; usufructuary and lessee only at PERCEPTIO.
• SEPARATIO = fruit detached from the fruit-bearing thing
• PERCEPTIO = gathering, i.e. taking possession
• Default rule: the owner acquires upon separation

cards.front: How and why does the BONAE FIDEI POSSESSOR acquire fruits?
cards.back:
At SEPARATIO, originally and free of liens, as a reward for his good faith and investment.
• He wrongly believes himself to be the owner
• Thief gets no wool from stolen sheep; bona fide buyer does (Case 104)

cards.front: A usucapient later learns the truth — does he still acquire fruits? (Pomponius/Paulus vs Julian)
cards.back:
Disputed: Pomponius and Paulus say no, Julian says yes until eviction.
• Pomponius/Paulus: usucaption continues (MALA FIDES SUPERVENIENS NON NOCET), fruits stop
• Julian: good faith at acquisition covers both until the owner sues

cards.front: Usufructuary and usufructuary lessee: who owns fruits between SEPARATIO and PERCEPTIO?
cards.back:
The owner of the fruit-bearing thing; usufructuary and lessee acquire only by PERCEPTIO.
• Only the owner can vindicate fruits taken by third parties
• Usufructuary: VINDICATIO USUSFRUCTUS; lessee: ACTIO CONDUCTI against lessor
• Lessee's acquisition is derivative (Example 26)

cards.front: What does ACCESSIO CEDIT PRINCIPALI mean?
cards.back:
The addition follows the main thing: its owner acquires the inseparably connected addition.
• He must compensate the former owner of the addition
• Good or bad faith of the connector irrelevant in rem
• Owners may agree otherwise, e.g. co-ownership

cards.front: Inseparable vs. severable connection — what is the difference and the consequence?
cards.back:
Inseparable if separation causes considerable damage or disproportionate effort; only then ownership passes.
• Interpenetration test: welding inseparable, soldering severable
• A tree is inseparable once it draws nutrients from the soil
• Severable: rights unaffected; ACTIO AD EXHIBENDUM, then REI VINDICATIO

cards.front: How do Roman jurists decide which thing is the main component?
cards.back:
By whether it can be claimed on its own by REI VINDICATIO, and by the nature of things.
• Writing cannot exist alone: it follows the parchment
• Statue with a welded arm: the statue is main
• Value and labour irrelevant (purple dye on wool)

cards.front: Which remedies has someone who lost ownership through ACCESSIO or SPECIFICATIO?
cards.back:
A claim for compensation against the new owner, or a defence if he still possesses.
• Good faith: ACTIO IN FACTUM (praetorian action describing the facts)
• Bad faith or theft: CONDICTIO FURTIVA
• In possession: EXCEPTIO DOLI against REI VINDICATIO until compensated

cards.front: Gai. 2.78 (Case 111): C paints on D's wooden panel (TABULA PICTA). Who owns the picture?
cards.back:
The painter: high-classical opinion lets the artistic contribution prevail, an exception to ACCESSIO CEDIT PRINCIPALI.
• Contrast: writing on another's parchment belongs to its owner (Case 110)
• Panel owner: EXCEPTIO DOLI, ACTIO UTILIS
• Gaius disagrees; late classical law treats painting like writing

cards.front: Paulus D 6.1.23.5 (Case 113): F's metal arm is soldered or welded to E's statue. Who owns the arm?
cards.back:
Soldered (ADPLUMBATIO): F keeps it; welded (FERRUMINATIO): E acquires it as owner of the main thing.
• Soldering: ACTIO AD EXHIBENDUM, then REI VINDICATIO
• Welding: F gets an ACTIO IN FACTUM for compensation
• If the arm later breaks off, it stays E's

cards.front: What does SUPERFICIES SOLO CEDIT mean?
cards.back:
What is firmly connected to land (SUPERFICIES) follows the legal fate of the land (SOLUM).
• Land is always the main component
• Historical origin of ACCESSIO CEDIT PRINCIPALI
• Covers IMPLANTATIO, SATIO, ALLUVIO, AEDIFICATIO

cards.front: Which cases of accession of movables to land does the textbook list?
cards.back:
IMPLANTATIO (planting), SATIO (sowing), ALLUVIO/AVULSIO (deposits) and AEDIFICATIO (building): the landowner acquires.
• Plant once it has taken root; seed once sown
• Deposits once firmly attached by a natural process
• Building only if on a fundament (movable granary stays builder's, Case 106)

cards.front: Why is AEDIFICATIO (building a house) an exception among accession cases?
cards.back:
Land and building form one entity, yet the materials remain a severable, latent accession.
• No ACTIO AD EXHIBENDUM to separate the materials
• DOMINIUM DORMIENS (dormant ownership) revives on demolition, ends with compensation
• Unlike SATIO/IMPLANTATIO, where acquisition is irrevocable

cards.front: Someone knowingly builds with his own materials on another's land — what can he claim?
cards.back:
No compensation, as he deserves no protection; he only has the IUS TOLLENDI.
• IUS TOLLENDI = right to remove (parts of) the building
• Only if this does not disadvantage the landowner

cards.front: Celsus D 6.1.38 (Case 107): F in good faith buys land from a non-owner, sows and builds; owner E vindicates. Result?
cards.back:
E gets the land but must reimburse F's expenses, at most the increase in value.
• Poor owner: F gets IUS TOLLENDI; E may pay the removal value instead
• NEQUE MALITIIS INDULGENDUM EST: no removal merely to destroy (chicanery)

cards.front: What is the ACTIO DE TIGNO IUNCTO?
cards.back:
Action against someone who builds on his own land with another's materials: he pays double (DUPLUM) their value.
• Only this constellation, not building on another's land
• Unclear: penal (owner keeps materials) or reipersecutory (ownership passes)

cards.front: CONFUSIO (blending) or COMMIXTIO (mixing) without the owners' consent — what happens to ownership?
cards.back:
Ownership continues: each owner claims his share by VINDICATIO PRO PARTE.
• Share by quantity or value (e.g. gold alloyed with copper)
• No ACTIO AD EXHIBENDUM and no compensation remedies needed

cards.front: Mixing without consent vs. mixing by mutual consent — which remedy?
cards.back:
Without consent: VINDICATIO PRO PARTE; with consent: COMMUNIO (co-ownership), dissolved by ACTIO COMMUNI DIVIDUNDO.
• After division each owner vindicates his allotted share

cards.front: A mixes B's coins indistinguishably with his own — who owns the money?
cards.back:
A acquires sole, original ownership, even as a thief.
• Reason: flexible cash management; coins are hard to trace
• B: unjust-enrichment CONDICTIO, or CONDICTIO FURTIVA against a thief
• With good-faith spending: NUMMOS CONSUMERE (using up coins)

cards.front: What is SPECIFICATIO (transformation)?
cards.back:
Creative transformation of another's object into a thing of a different nature.
• Product looks different and usually bears a different name
• Key question: is identity determined by material or by form?

cards.front: Transformation vs. processing vs. accession — examples with Titus' wool?
cards.back:
Making clothes = SPECIFICATIO; cleaning = processing; dyeing with one's own purple = ACCESSIO.
• Processing: no substantial change, no effect on ownership
• Dyed wool stays Titus' (accession)

cards.front: Sabinians vs. Proculians on SPECIFICATIO — who owns the new product and why?
cards.back:
Sabinians: the owner of the material; Proculians: the maker, who occupies a new RES NULLIUS.
• Sabinians: MATERIA MANENS — SINE MATERIA NULLA SPECIES EFFICI POSSIT
• Proculians: form decides — QUOD FACTUM EST, ANTEA NULLIUS FUERAT

cards.front: What does the MEDIA SENTENTIA on SPECIFICATIO say (Gaius D 41.1.7.7)?
cards.back:
Reversible transformation: owner of the material (Sabinian); irreversible: the maker acquires originally (Proculian).
• Reversibility judged abstractly (metal can be melted down)
• Maker includes one acting ALIENO NOMINE (in his name)
• Not if done by mutual consent (LOCATIO CONDUCTIO OPERIS)

cards.front: Gaius D 41.1.7.7 (Case 120): vessel from B's metal, ship from planks, wine from grapes, threshed corn — who owns?
cards.back:
Metal vessel: owner of the metal (reversible); ship, clothes, mead, salve, oil, wine: the maker (irreversible).
• Threshed grain: owner of the ears
• Threshing creates nothing new, it only reveals what exists

cards.front: Exegesis: a Digest fragment is about ACCESSIO or SPECIFICATIO — which questions should your interpretation address?
cards.back:
Classify the case first: ACCESSIO, mixing, or SPECIFICATIO?
• Inseparable connection? Main thing (REI VINDICATIO test)?
• Land (SUPERFICIES SOLO CEDIT, AEDIFICATIO)? Reversible transformation (MEDIA SENTENTIA)?
• Good or bad faith → ACTIO IN FACTUM, CONDICTIO FURTIVA, EXCEPTIO DOLI?
